title: Using neural networks to fill in post-Newtonian terms cuts training data by ten thousand times
dek: A pure neural network waveform model needs 10^8 to 10^10 training waveforms, but writing known physics into the network and letting it learn only the corrections requires just 8 numerical relativity waveforms.
why: The first half covers the state of the field in gravitational wave modeling; the second half on surrogate acceleration and the specific numbers for PINNs is more worth hearing.
who: Graduate students and engineers working on gravitational wave data analysis, numerical relativity, or scientific machine learning, especially those who want to use physics constraints to reduce training data.
skip: The first ~5 minutes of conference introduction and detector sensitivity curve background can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: LIGO's error bars may come from theory, not the instrument
points.body: The speaker says that for some LIGO events, it cannot be ruled out that the analysis results are limited by understanding of waveform systematic errors, not just cryogenic cooling or mirror defects. GW23123 is an example: running different models produces non-trivial differences in the posterior distributions. His position is not to take sides on who is right, but to provide better error bars for the models, letting the data analysts continue to argue about who is right.

points.h: Double the simulation length, quadruple the error
points.body: The mismatch of numerical relativity simulations scales roughly as the square of the wavelength. Because simulation accuracy is dominated by phase error, phase error accumulates linearly with time, and mismatch is the square of phase error. So wanting a simulation twice as long is not just waiting longer; you also have to make it more accurate, and the cost is multiplicatively punishing. Currently most simulations fall around 30 orbits, while the reference line is about 25 orbits.

points.h: For next-generation detectors, pure numerical relativity has no hope
points.body: The speaker showed a plot: the horizontal axis is event signal-to-noise ratio, the vertical axis is the number of simulations in the catalog with sufficient accuracy and length. For LIGO, about 85% to 90% of the catalog is sufficient, about 3000 simulations; but for heavy systems at 10^4 signal-to-noise ratio, only about 10 simulations in total are sufficient. For Cosmic Explorer and Einstein Telescope, the conclusion is that numerical relativity alone is completely insufficient, and other models are needed to fill in.

points.h: Hybrid waveforms are actually stitching together two different physical systems
points.body: When stitching post-Newtonian waveforms with numerical relativity waveforms, the cost function has many local minima in parameter space, and the global minimum falls in a narrow, shallow valley that optimizers struggle to find. The test method is to run a simulation of about 60 orbits, then shift the matching window to see what the early waveform looks like. The result is that the early numerical relativity waveform and the post-Newtonian waveform look completely different, equivalent to smoothly stitching together waveforms from two different physical systems, introducing bias.

points.h: Let the neural network learn only what post-Newtonian cannot compute
points.body: Each additional post-Newtonian term is a PhD thesis worth of work, so the speaker's idea is to treat the neural network as encoding all the post-Newtonian terms he does not want to write by hand. The network needs only about 100 parameters, about 120 CPU hours of training, and only 8 numerical relativity waveforms in mass ratio space. In addition to waveform difference, the loss function also requires orbital velocity to be close, the correction term to vanish as orbital velocity goes to zero, and equal-mass symmetry and weight regularization.

points.h: Physics-informed networks extrapolate better outside the training set
points.body: At a point outside the training set, mass ratio 9 to 5, post-Newtonian completely fails near merger, the surrogate model (trained up to mass ratio 8) has growing extrapolation error, while the physics-informed neural network performs much better. If after training up to mass ratio 8 you add one data point at mass ratio 15, the error all the way up to mass ratio 15 drops substantially. This promises to reduce the amount of training data needed to build models.

points.h: Pure neural network approaches need over ten thousand times more training data
points.body: The speaker says that most other attempts he has seen at modeling waveforms with neural networks completely abandon physics and use only neural networks or autoencoders, which really need 10^8 to 10^10 waveforms for training, meaning you would first have to build a surrogate to generate the training data, because it is impossible to obtain that many numerical relativity waveforms. His conclusion: machine learning is a useful tool, but do not forget that you actually know something about what you are modeling.

points.h: Surrogate speedup of 30 to 40 times comes from changing the algorithm
points.body: The speaker says all he did was make the code less bad, with no revolutionary insight. The starting point was about 30 milliseconds, now about 30 to 40 times faster. The biggest speedup came from changing the algorithm: from cubic interpolation to tenth-order Hermite polynomials, with far fewer time nodes. Currently the dynamics part dominates, about 370 microseconds, while waveform evaluation takes only 50 microseconds. He estimates that ultimately a 0.2 millisecond frequency-domain waveform can be produced, comparable to or better than the fastest phenom waveforms.
